items.prompt: We’ve seen that this fraction 5/6 is made up of five sixths. We can write that as a sum. My turn first: this is five sixths, so I write one sixth five times, added together.

items.demo: Three sixths, so I write one sixth three times. *3/6 = 1/6 + 1/6 + 1/6*.
Three fourths, so I write one fourth three times. *3/4 = 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4*. Each time, the bottom number tells us which unit fraction to write, and the top number tells us how many of them to add.

items.prompt: Your turn. Express four fifths as a sum of unit fractions.  4/5
items.demo: Four fifths, so I write one fifth four times: *4/5 = 1/5 + 1/5 + 1/5 + 1/5*.

items.prompt: Express two fifths as a sum of unit fractions.  2/5
items.demo: Two fifths, so I write one fifth two times: *2/5 = 1/5 + 1/5*.

items.prompt: Express two sevenths as a sum of unit fractions.  2/7
items.demo: Two sevenths, so I write one seventh two times: *2/7 = 1/7 + 1/7*.

items.prompt: Express seven thirds as a sum of unit fractions.  7/3
items.demo: Seven thirds, so I write one third seven times: *7/3 = 1/3 + 1/3 + 1/3 + 1/3 + 1/3 + 1/3 + 1/3*.

items.prompt: Express one eighth as a sum of unit fractions.  1/8
items.demo: One eighth is already a unit fraction: *1/8*.

items.prompt: Express three over one as a sum of unit fractions.  3/1
items.demo: Three over one, so I write one over one three times: *3/1 = 1/1 + 1/1 + 1/1*.

items.prompt: Here is a sum. Write it as a single fraction.

Priya says three fifths is one fifth can be written like this:  3/5 = 1/5 + 1/5 + 1/5  add one fifth, add one fifth. Ben says three fifths is written like this:  3/5 = 3/5 + 3/5 + 3/5  three fifths, add three fifths, add three fifths. Who is right? How do you know?
items.demo: *Priya*. Each part counted is one fifth, so we add one fifth three times.
